The support FAQ, product guide, and customer interviews collectively describe scanned PDFs as image-only files that need Optical Character Recognition (OCR) before KnowledgeHub can extract text or generate reliable citations.

- **Support FAQ**: Scanned PDFs require OCR; without OCR they cannot be searched and citations cannot be generated. The standard parser only reads digital text layers, so an unprocessed scanned PDF extracts zero text. OCR is heuristic and can misread blurry/low-resolution scans, handwriting, or complex layouts, causing broken citations, knowledge gaps, and longer processing times. Recommended resolutions include checking if OCR is enabled, exporting a text-searchable PDF from the source system instead of scanning, or using the Advanced OCR Pipeline for Enterprise/Growth customers [NL-006#NL-006-S03]. It also advises converting tables to `.csv`/`.xlsx` or using clear grid lines to avoid garbled table OCR, and notes standard OCR ignores handwriting/annotations [NL-006#NL-006-S03].

- **Product guide**: PDF is the default format, and scanned or image-only PDFs require OCR processing; other formats such as DOCX, Markdown, and CSV have higher citation precision and are recommended alternatives [NL-002#NL-002-S08].

- **Customer interviews**: Enterprise customers report that 40–50% of their files are scanned PDFs without text layers, leading to missing citations or citations pointing to whole documents, which violates reliability expectations and lowers CSAT [NL-021#NL-021-S02]. BrightPath similarly reports about 45% of its corpus is scanned image-only PDFs, causing poor citation quality; NovaLearn recommends exporting original DOCX files, excluding scans from the pilot, or waiting for the Advanced OCR Pipeline scheduled for August 2026 [NL-024#NL-024-S04]. Another customer describes manually running OCR before upload as a massive resource drain across thousands of pages, and requests automated OCR with validation so clinical editors can review extracted text [NL-018#NL-018-S05]. Acme also wants automated OCR instead of manual pre-processing and is waiting for the August pipeline [NL-017#NL-017-S06].

Collectively, the sources agree that scanned PDFs are a major ingestion pain point; they require OCR to become searchable, manual OCR pre-processing is burdensome, and the planned Advanced OCR Pipeline is expected to automate this while improving citation granularity.
